Their sidecars
Homepage and Uptime Kuma get read access to the services they watch; nothing else reaches out.


tag:homeassistant
Home Assistant (applied in the admin console, so the HA Tailscale app’s Advertise tags option stays empty)
Household on 443/8123.


tag:dockhand, tag:dockhand-offsite
Dockhand’s sidecar on each TrueNAS
Kept on their own tags: Dockhand is effectively root on the box. ACL tests assert nothing else can reach them.


tag:jetkvm, tag:pfsense, tag:media-client
Out-of-band KVM, the router, the SHIELD
Admin-only (KVM, pfSense) / Jellyfin client.



Principals: group:admin (me) gets *:*, which is why admin-only UIs need no per-service grant. group:household gets 443 on the family tags and Home Assistant. The policy’s tests block pins the important denials (k8s nodes can’t reach the backup box or Dockhand, household can’t reach Dockhand or the TrueNAS UI, and so on); add a test whenever a new tag is introduced.
Two subtleties:

Why tag:k8s and tag:k8s-node are separate. The operator’s defaultTags sets the tag on Ingress devices; Talos nodes advertise their own via TS_EXTRA_ARGS. Nodes need NFS to tag:truenas-primary; operator devices need to be reachable from personal devices. One tag would over-grant both ways.
What tags don’t cover. Tailscale only governs tailnet traffic. A container can still reach the LAN (TrueNAS UI, pfSense, Home Assistant) through Docker’s bridge NAT. That gap is handled by container hardening (see “Container hardening and supply chain” below), not by the ACL.


democratic-csi controller traffic to TrueNAS
The democratic-csi NFS driver needs to call the TrueNAS HTTPS API to create/destroy datasets. With TrueNAS only reachable over Tailscale, the controller pod also has to take that path. Two changes make this work:

controller.hostNetwork: true on the democratic-csi Helm release, so the controller pod sits on the node’s network namespace and can use the node’s tailscale0 interface.
An ExternalName Service (truenas-tailscale) in the democratic-csi namespace, annotated for the Tailscale operator to resolve to the TrueNAS tailnet IP. The driver’s HTTPS API host points at that Service (keeping the IP out of the SOPS-encrypted config). Note the NFS shareHost is still a bare tailnet IP — it gets baked into each PV at provision time, which is why repointing storage to a different TrueNAS requires re-adopting the existing PVs (see docs/storage-migration.md), not just a config edit.

This is documented inline in kubernetes/infrastructure/democratic-csi/truenas-egress.yaml.

title: Architecture
text:
Container hardening and supply chain
Nothing is exposed to the internet, so the realistic ways in are a malicious or hijacked image, or a parser bug in an app that handles files from strangers (qBittorrent, the *arrs, Jellyfin’s ffmpeg, Kavita, RomM, Paperless OCR). The layers, from “stop it arriving” to “limit the damage”:

Pinned images, reviewed updates. Every image is pinned to an exact release in its docker-compose.yml (no latest, no *_VERSION in .env). Renovate opens a weekly PR per update with a 5-day minimumReleaseAge, so a hijacked release usually gets caught upstream before it’s even proposed. Merging is the deploy trigger (Dockhand’s git sync; the Frigate LXC, outside Dockhand, pulls main with an hourly timer); Dockhand’s own image auto-update is off. Databases stay on their current major; Immich’s Postgres follows Immich’s notes.
Vulnerability scanning. Dockhand scans images (Grype/Trivy) during its update checks; counts by severity feed the Homelab – security Grafana dashboard and the dockhand alert group. Scanners find known CVEs, mostly in base-image packages; they don’t detect malware.
Least privilege per container. no-new-privileges on every service except Alloy (privileged by design, for node/cAdvisor metrics) and Frigate. Newer stacks (radicale, games, reading, docs-site) also drop all capabilities and run as 568 directly; extending cap_drop: ALL to the older linuxserver-based services is a per-service job, since their init needs CHOWN/SETUID/SETGID.
Network containment. Databases and caches (Immich, Paperless, RomM) sit on internal: true networks with no gateway: no internet, no LAN. On the tailnet, sidecars are tagged and the policy is default-deny (see above). The remaining gap is LAN egress from app containers, which Docker NATs as the TrueNAS host; closing it would need host firewall rules that TrueNAS updates overwrite, so it’s accepted.
Recovery. ZFS snapshots can’t be touched from inside a container, and replication carries them off-site: the backstop for anything that gets through.

Trust is uneven: small single-maintainer images (Suggestarr, ROMarr, Bookshelf) get read before their updates are merged, and none of them mount Immich or Paperless data.

title: Architecture
text:
Secrets management

Strategy overview








Platform
Method
Where secrets live




TrueNAS (Docker)
.env files (never committed)
On the host only


Kubernetes (Flux)
SOPS + age (encrypted in git)
Cluster only (private key)





SOPS + age: how it works
SOPS encrypts individual YAML values (not the whole file) using a recipient’s public key. The encrypted file is safe to commit; decryption requires the corresponding private key, which lives only inside the cluster.
age provides the key pair:
age-keygen -o age.agekey
# Public key:  age1sg49q...   ← stored in .sops.yaml (safe to commit)
# Private key: AGE-SECRET-...  ← stored only in the cluster as a K8s Secret
The private key is bootstrapped into the cluster once:
kubectl create secret generic sops-age \
  --namespace=flux-system \
  --from-file=age.agekey=./age.agekey
After that, the local copy is deleted (or stored in a password manager as a break-glass recovery key). Flux’s decryption stanza in apps.yaml tells it to use this secret when reconciling:
decryption:
  provider: sops
  secretRef:
    name: sops-age


Secret lifecycle
1. Author creates secret file:
   kubernetes/apps/<ns>/<app>/<name>-secret.sops.yaml

2. Fill in plaintext values (DO NOT COMMIT at this stage)

3. Encrypt in place:
   sops --encrypt --in-place kubernetes/apps/<ns>/<app>/<name>-secret.sops.yaml

4. Commit the encrypted file — values are AES-256-GCM ciphertext,
   safe to store in a public repository.

5. On git push, Flux fetches the file, decrypts it in-cluster using
   the age private key, and applies the resulting Secret to Kubernetes.

6. To edit later:
   sops kubernetes/apps/<ns>/<app>/<name>-secret.sops.yaml
   # Opens $EDITOR with plaintext; re-encrypts on save.


Defence in depth against accidental plaintext commits
Three independent layers protect against committing unencrypted secrets:

Naming convention — all Kubernetes secrets use the .sops.yaml suffix, making them visually distinguishable and easy to pattern-match in hooks and gitignore rules.
check-sops-encrypted pre-commit hook — deterministic check: any staged *.sops.yaml file that lacks the sops: block (which SOPS adds on encryption) causes the commit to fail with a clear error message. This is the primary safety net.
Gitleaks — catches other accidentally committed secrets using entropy analysis and known pattern matching. Complements the SOPS hook but is not SOPS-aware; the two hooks cover different failure modes.



Trust boundaries
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Git repository (public)                                       │
│  *.sops.yaml  ← AES-256-GCM ciphertext, safe to store here  │
│  .sops.yaml   ← age PUBLIC key only, safe to store here      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │ Flux pulls + decrypts
                              ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Kubernetes cluster (flux-system namespace)                    │
│  Secret/sops-age  ← age PRIVATE key, never leaves cluster    │
│                                                               │
│  Flux decrypts *.sops.yaml in memory; plaintext Secret       │
│  objects are applied to the cluster but never written to git  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
The age private key is the only secret that cannot be rotated via git. It should be backed up to a password manager as a break-glass recovery key in case the cluster is destroyed and needs to be rebuilt from scratch.

title: Talos system extensions rollout
text:
Status (2026-06-15): legacy / pre-cutover reference.
This runbook was written for the original hand-built 1-control-plane + 2-worker Talos cluster whose machine configs lived in proxmox/. That cluster has been replaced by a 3-CP + 2-worker cluster provisioned by OpenTofu (see opentofu/README.md).
On the OpenTofu cluster, extension changes are made by editing the talos_extensions variable in opentofu/live/homelab/main.tf and running tofu apply — the talos-image module re-derives the Image Factory schematic ID and the talos-cluster module rolls nodes one at a time via staged_if_needing_reboot. There is no need for the manual talosctl patch + talosctl upgrade choreography below.
The text below is retained because (1) it documents the step-by-step reasoning for what each phase of an extension rollout actually does, which remains educational, and (2) the proxmox/ cluster is kept powered off as a quick rollback option until the new cluster has been stable for long enough.
Paths in proxmox/ referenced below no longer exist in the OpenTofu world; their equivalents live under opentofu/modules/talos-cluster/patches/.
This runbook covers installing or updating Talos Linux system extensions on the existing cluster — specifically the first rollout of siderolabs/tailscale (joining each node to the tailnet so kubelet can mount NFS from off-site TrueNAS), but the procedure is the same for any future extension change.
It is written for the legacy cluster topology: one control plane node and two workers. With a single control plane, the API server is unavailable during the few minutes the control plane reboots. This is acceptable for a homelab but worth being aware of — kubectl and Flux will both fail until the control plane is back, then catch up automatically.

title: Talos system extensions rollout
text:
Why a runbook
Extension changes happen rarely, and the steps are easy to get subtly wrong. Capturing the order of operations and the reasoning for each step makes future rollouts repeatable rather than improvised.

title: Talos system extensions rollout
text:
Prerequisites
A shell with these variables set (the values below are the current cluster — update as needed):
export CONTROL_PLANE_IP=192.168.1.31
export WORKER_IPS=("192.168.1.32" "192.168.1.33")
export SCHEMATIC=077514df2c1b6436460bc60faabc976687b16193b8a1290fda4366c69024fec2
export TALOSCONFIG=proxmox/talosconfig
SCHEMATIC is the Image Factory ID for the bundle of extensions defined in proxmox/schematic.yaml. If that file changes, regenerate the ID:
curl -X POST --data-binary @proxmox/schematic.yaml \
  https://factory.talos.dev/schematics
# {"id":"<new-id>"}
Schematic IDs are deterministic — the same schematic.yaml always produces the same ID — so this is safe to re-run.
You also need an out-of-band recovery path in case the control plane fails to come back. For this cluster that’s Proxmox console access to the Talos VMs (Talos exposes a recovery TUI on the VM console). For the TrueNAS host that NFS lives on, the equivalent is JetKVM.

title: Talos system extensions rollout
text:
Step 1 — Pre-flight checks
Confirm what’s actually running on each node, not just what the machine config claims:
talosctl version --nodes "$CONTROL_PLANE_IP"
for n in $WORKER_IPS; do talosctl version --nodes "$n"; done
Note the server Talos version for each node. The upgrade target should match this version unless you’re intentionally bumping Talos — mixing an extension rollout with a Talos version bump doubles the blast radius if something goes wrong, so do them as separate rollouts.
Check cluster health:
talosctl --nodes $CONTROL_PLANE_IP health
This must report healthy before continuing. If it doesn’t, fix the underlying issue first — upgrading an unhealthy cluster is asking for trouble.
Confirm Flux is in a clean state:
flux get all -A
If any Kustomization or HelmRelease is reconciling or failing, let it settle (or suspend it) before the upgrade. Mid-reconciliation + API-server outage during the CP reboot can leave Flux state confused.

title: Talos system extensions rollout
text:
Step 2 — Snapshot etcd
With a single control plane, etcd has no replicas to recover from. Take a snapshot before touching it:
talosctl etcd snapshot etcd-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).db \
  --endpoints "$CONTROL_PLANE_IP" \
  --nodes "$CONTROL_PLANE_IP"
Store the snapshot somewhere off the control plane node — at minimum copy it to your laptop or workstation. If the upgrade destroys etcd and you only have the snapshot on the same VM, you have nothing.

title: Talos system extensions rollout
section: Step 3 — Compose the installer image URL
text:
Step 3 — Compose the installer image URL
# Match this to the server version observed in Step 1
export TALOS_VERSION=v1.13.2
export INSTALLER="factory.talos.dev/installer/${SCHEMATIC}:${TALOS_VERSION}"
echo "$INSTALLER"
Sanity check by pulling the image manifest (optional but cheap):
docker manifest inspect "$INSTALLER"

title: Talos system extensions rollout
text:
Step 4 — Apply the ExtensionServiceConfig patch
Before upgrading to an image that contains a new extension, push the extension’s runtime configuration to each node. For siderolabs/tailscale this is proxmox/tailscale-extension.yaml, which sets TS_AUTHKEY and TS_EXTRA_ARGS. The patch is harmless to apply ahead of the upgrade — Talos will only act on it once the extension is actually present on the node.
talosctl patch machineconfig \
  --nodes "$CONTROL_PLANE_IP" \
  --patch @proxmox/tailscale-extension.yaml

for ip in "${WORKER_IPS[@]}"; do
    talosctl patch machineconfig \
      --nodes "$ip" \
      --patch @proxmox/tailscale-extension.yaml
done

title: Talos system extensions rollout
section: Step 5 — Upgrade the workers, then the control plane
text:
Step 5 — Upgrade the workers, then the control plane
Workers first, one at a time, so the cluster only ever has one node draining. Save the control plane for last — with a single CP this is the API-server outage window, and you want to know workers are happy before you take it.
for ip in "${WORKER_IPS[@]}"; do
    talosctl upgrade --nodes "$ip" --image "$INSTALLER"
    # Wait for the node to come back Ready before moving on
    talosctl health --nodes "$ip"
done

talosctl upgrade --nodes "$CONTROL_PLANE_IP" --image "$INSTALLER"

title: Talos system extensions rollout
section: Step 6 — Verify the extension is loaded
text:
Step 6 — Verify the extension is loaded
talosctl get extensions --nodes "$CONTROL_PLANE_IP"
for n in "${WORKER_IPS[@]}"; do talosctl get extensions --nodes "$n"; done
Each node should list siderolabs/tailscale along with the other extensions defined in proxmox/schematic.yaml (currently iscsi-tools, qemu-guest-agent, util-linux-tools).

title: Talos system extensions rollout
section: Step 6a — kubelet nodeIP patch (one-time, only on first rollout)
text:
Step 6a — kubelet nodeIP patch (one-time, only on first rollout)
The first time the tailscale extension comes up on a node, kubelet may pick the new tailscale0 interface IP (100.x.y.z) as its nodeIP, because Talos by default uses the first non-loopback IPv4. This breaks Flux and anything else that talks to the kubelet over the LAN, because node-to-node traffic now tries to route via DERP.
The fix is to pin kubelet’s nodeIP to the LAN subnet via proxmox/patch-node-ip.yaml:
machine:
  kubelet:
    nodeIP:
      validSubnets:
        - 192.168.1.0/24
Apply it and reboot all nodes:
talosctl patch machineconfig -p @proxmox/patch-node-ip.yaml \
  --nodes "$CONTROL_PLANE_IP" --endpoints "$CONTROL_PLANE_IP"
for ip in "${WORKER_IPS[@]}"; do
    talosctl patch machineconfig -p @proxmox/patch-node-ip.yaml \
      --nodes "$ip" --endpoints "$CONTROL_PLANE_IP"
done

talosctl reboot \
  --nodes "$CONTROL_PLANE_IP,${WORKER_IPS[0]},${WORKER_IPS[1]}" \
  --endpoints "$CONTROL_PLANE_IP"
This patch is now part of the baseline machine config, so it only needs re-applying if you add new nodes or wipe an existing one.

title: Talos system extensions rollout
text:
Step 7 — Verify
Per-node service status:
talosctl service ext-tailscale --nodes "$CONTROL_PLANE_IP"
for n in $WORKER_IPS; do talosctl service ext-tailscale --nodes "$n"; done
State should be Running and health OK. If health is unhealthy, pull logs:
talosctl logs ext-tailscale --nodes "$CONTROL_PLANE_IP"
Common reasons it fails:

Auth key is wrong, expired, or not tagged with tag:k8s-node.
Auth key not marked Pre-approved and your tailnet requires manual device approval.
ACL doesn’t grant tag:k8s-node ownership to anything (check tagOwners in the ACL).

In the Tailscale admin console → Machines, each node should appear with its hostname (Talos node name) and tag:k8s-node. This is the authoritative “did it work” check — Talos doesn’t ship the tailscale CLI on the node (no shell, no userland), so admin console + ACL tests are the verification surface.
Tailnet-side reachability is verified from another tailnet device (your laptop):
# Find the node's tailnet IP in the admin console, then:
tailscale ping <node-tailnet-ip>
ssh into the node is not possible — this is just a reachability test
tailscale ping will indicate whether the connection is direct or via a relay (DERP). Either is functional, but direct is preferable for NFS throughput. If everything resolves over DERP, check that UDP 41641 is reachable inbound to your nodes on the Proxmox host firewall.

title: Talos system extensions rollout
section: Step 8 — Update the ACL (if not done already)
text:
Step 8 — Update the ACL (if not done already)
This is covered in docs/architecture.md and the Tailscale section of the repo, but for completeness: with nodes now tagged tag:k8s-node, the grant they rely on is
{
  "src": ["tag:k8s-node"],
  "dst": ["tag:truenas"],
  "ip":  ["tcp:2049"]
}
The end-to-end test is to apply a small NFS PV/PVC in the cluster and confirm a test pod mounts it successfully. That belongs in the democratic-csi rollout runbook rather than this one, but as a quick smoke test you can deploy a throwaway pod with an nfs volume pointing at the TrueNAS tailnet IP. If the pod reaches Running, the kubelet on its host successfully completed the NFS mount over Tailscale.

title: Talos system extensions rollout
text:
Rollback
If something goes wrong at any step, the rollback path is:

Before Step 4 (CP upgrade): nothing to roll back, just stop.
During or after Step 4, CP unhealthy: restore etcd from the snapshot taken in Step 2. The Talos recovery procedure is:

Reset the control plane node, wiping STATE and EPHEMERAL: talosctl reset --graceful=false --reboot --system-labels-to-wipe STATE,EPHEMERAL --nodes "$CONTROL_PLANE_IP"
Re-apply the machine config (back to the previous stock installer image, e.g. ghcr.io/siderolabs/installer:v1.13.0 — no schematic): talosctl apply-config --insecure --nodes "$CONTROL_PLANE_IP" --file proxmox/controlplane.yaml
Bootstrap from the snapshot: talosctl bootstrap --recover-from etcd-backup-<timestamp>.db --nodes "$CONTROL_PLANE_IP"

Full recovery details are in the Talos docs under “Disaster Recovery”; the procedure has subtle version-specific differences so cross-check before running it under pressure.
After Step 5, worker unhealthy: workers can be wiped and rejoined via talosctl reset --graceful=false --reboot followed by re-applying the worker machine config. The cluster tolerates a worker being out for the duration.
After Step 6, Tailscale service crashlooping: the extension being unhealthy does not affect Kubernetes — the node continues to function for everything that doesn’t need the tailnet. Fix the auth key or ACL and re-apply Step 6. There’s no need to roll back the upgrade.

The worst-case scenario — control plane unrecoverable, etcd snapshot corrupt — is a full cluster rebuild. The Flux GitOps repo means workloads come back automatically once a new cluster is bootstrapped and pointed at the same Git repo. Volume state (NFS) is unaffected because it lives on TrueNAS.

title: Talos system extensions rollout
text:
Notes for future runs

This runbook can be re-used unchanged when schematic.yaml is amended to add or remove an extension. Just regenerate the schematic ID in Step 1 and re-run.
It can also be re-used for Talos minor version upgrades — change TALOS_VERSION in Step 3. Do not combine an extension change and a Talos version bump in the same rollout if it can be avoided.
The ExtensionServiceConfig in Step 6 only needs to be re-applied when its content changes (new auth key, new TS_EXTRA_ARGS). It is idempotent — re-applying the same config is a no-op.
The current single-CP topology is a deliberate homelab compromise. If the cluster ever grows to three control plane nodes, the rolling upgrade in Step 4 becomes non-disruptive and --preserve can be dropped.

Grafana Alloy for every Docker host in the homelab. The same files run on each box; only .env differs. Ships:
Both go to the cluster’s push-only endpoints (kubernetes/apps/monitoring/ingest-ingress.yaml) over the tailnet. Read them in Grafana (Explore → Loki: {host="<HOST_LABEL>"}; the Node Exporter Full and Cadvisor dashboards in the Homelab folder have a host picker).
The stack lives under truenas/ for history (moving it would orphan the primary’s Dockhand stack and its Tailscale state); it is not TrueNAS-specific.

title: Alloy
text:
Deploy

Tailscale admin: a single-use, pre-approved, non-ephemeral auth key tagged tag:monitoring-agent, one per box. (The policy grant tag:monitoring-agent → tag:monitoring-ingest:443 already exists.)
Fill .env from .env.example with the row above.

Dockhand: add the stack pointed at this directory, paste the .env in its UI, deploy.
Plain Docker (Frigate LXC, repo cloned at /root/homelab):
cd /root/homelab && git pull
cd truenas/docker-compose/alloy
cp .env.example .env && chmod 600 .env   # then edit it
docker compose up -d
.env and ts-state/ are gitignored, so git pull keeps working. Update later with git pull && docker compose up -d.

Check: alloy-ts joins the tailnet as TS_HOSTNAME; docker logs alloy shows no loki.write / remote_write errors; in Grafana, {host="<HOST_LABEL>"} returns logs and up{host="<HOST_LABEL>"} is 1.

Alloy’s debug UI listens on 127.0.0.1:12345 of each host only (e.g. ssh -L 12345:127.0.0.1:12345 root@<box>).

title: Alloy
text:
pfSense (via the Frigate LXC)
pfSense can’t run Alloy, so the Frigate LXC’s Alloy collects for it. Two optional .env values, set only there:








Variable
Frigate LXC
Elsewhere




SYSLOG_LISTEN_ADDR
192.168.1.39:1514 (UDP syslog listener on its LAN IP)
unset → 127.0.0.1:1514, receives nothing


PFSENSE_EXPORTER
<pfSense LAN IP>:9100 (node_exporter package)
unset → no target



Logs arrive as {host="pfsense", job="syslog"} with unit = program (filterlog, unbound, dhcpd, sshd, php-fpm, …) and level; metrics as up{host="pfsense"}. FreeBSD’s node_exporter names some memory and disk metrics differently, so parts of the Node Exporter Full dashboard stay empty.
pfSense side:

Status → System Logs → Settings:

Log Message Format: syslog (RFC 5424).
Enable Remote Logging, Source Address: LAN, IP Protocol: IPv4, Remote log servers: 192.168.1.39:1514, Remote Syslog Contents: Everything (untick firewall events if filterlog is too noisy).

System → Package Manager: install the node_exporter package, enable it under its Services page, listening on the LAN interface only, port 9100.

The syslog listener has no authentication, so the Frigate LXC drops UDP 1514 from anything but pfSense with an nftables rule in its own table (syslog-allow-pfsense.nft; install steps in its header). Every stream gets a fixed host="pfsense" label, never the sender-supplied hostname.

title: Alloy
text:
Dockhand (TrueNAS boxes)
Each TrueNAS box’s Alloy also scrapes that box’s Dockhand /metrics: vulnerability counts by severity, images scanned, pending updates, container health and restarts, scheduled task and backup status. They land as {job="dockhand", host="<box>"} with Dockhand’s own env label, feeding the Homelab – security dashboard and the dockhand group in kubernetes/apps/monitoring/alert-rules.yaml. Two optional .env values, set only on the TrueNAS boxes:








Variable
Primary TrueNAS
Elsewhere (Quack01 included)




DOCKHAND_METRICS
127.0.0.1:30328 (the Dockhand app’s node-port)
unset → no target


DOCKHAND_TOKEN
API token from the primary’s Dockhand
unset



Quack01 is deliberately not scraped: dockhand-offsite.yml publishes no port at all (it’s on the family LAN and Dockhand is root-equivalent), and Alloy on the host network can’t reach it any other way. A loopback-only publish was considered and rejected: Docker before 28 lets other hosts on the same L2 segment reach 127.0.0.1-published ports. Revisit if the off-site box’s scan data starts to matter (e.g. Alloy joining the Dockhand app’s network).
/metrics stays behind Dockhand’s login. Dockhand accepts an API token as Authorization: Bearer dh_... on /metrics (as on /api/*), so Alloy sends that; EXPORT_METRICS_PUBLIC is deliberately not used (on the primary it would open the endpoint to the whole LAN through the 0.0.0.0 node-port).
Per box:

Turn the endpoint on. Primary: TrueNAS → Apps → Dockhand → Edit → add the environment variable EXPORT_METRICS = true, save (the app restarts).
Create a token. In that box’s Dockhand: Profile → API tokens → new, name it alloy-metrics. It acts as the user who created it (any authenticated user can read /metrics), so if you have a non-admin user, create it there. An expiry is fine, but when it lapses the scrape gets 401 and DockhandMetricsDown fires; rotate before then.
Give it to Alloy. Add DOCKHAND_METRICS and DOCKHAND_TOKEN to the stack’s .env in Dockhand, redeploy.
Check. In Grafana, up{job="dockhand", host="<box>"} is 1 and dockhand_vulnerabilities has series. Otherwise, on the box, curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:30328/metrics: 404 = EXPORT_METRICS isn’t on, 401 = on (so a 401 in docker logs alloy is the token), connection refused = wrong port.

text:
Not covered here
Hosts without Docker (the Proxmox hosts) run Alloy as a system package with their own config: see proxmox-hosts/.

title: Dockhand (off-site)
text: A separate Dockhand on Quack01 that deploys its git stacks (uptime-kuma, alloy). Separate on purpose: an agent of the primary’s Dockhand would give the primary root on the backup box. Why the YAML looks the way it does is in the header of dockhand-offsite.yml.

title: Dockhand (off-site)
text:
Install

Dataset HDDs/dockhand with two empty directories inside: data/ and ts-state/.
Tailscale admin: add "tag:dockhand-offsite": ["autogroup:admin"] to tagOwners, then a single-use, pre-approved, non-ephemeral auth key with that tag. Its own tag, not the primary’s tag:dockhand, so a grant written for one Dockhand never silently covers the other. Owner access needs no grant; nothing else should get one.
TrueNAS → Apps → Discover → ⋮ → Install via YAML: paste dockhand-offsite.yml, replace tskey-auth-REPLACE_ME there (not in git), name the app dockhand, save.
Open https://dockhand-offsite.<tailnet>.ts.net and create the admin user straight away: until then the UI has no login, and anything the tailnet lets reach it on 443 (today that includes tag:uptime-kuma, whose grant is dst: ["*"]) could claim it.
Add this repo (public, no credentials) and create the git stacks, each with its .env pasted in Dockhand:

truenas/docker-compose/uptime-kuma (off-site values in its .env.example)
truenas/docker-compose/alloy (HOST_LABEL=quack01)


Leave auto-update off, as on the primary: Pull → review → Redeploy.

title: Dockhand (off-site)
text:
Updating Dockhand itself
Bump the two pinned image tags in dockhand-offsite.yml, commit, then paste the new YAML into the app’s Edit screen in TrueNAS.

title: Docs site
text: This repo’s documentation as a browsable website: docs/*.md, the architecture diagrams and every stack README, with a sidebar and search. Tailnet-only, at https://docs.<tailnet>.ts.net.

title: Docs site
text:
How it works
push to main ──► GitHub Actions: quarto render ──► docs-html branch (HTML only)
                                                        │  every 5 min
TrueNAS: docs-site-sync (git fetch) ──► html volume ──► nginx ──► tailscale serve

Source: the Markdown stays where it is. _quarto.yml at the repo root lists what goes on the site; index.qmd pulls in the top-level README as the home page. The Markdown still reads normally on GitHub (```mermaid fences are turned into diagrams by docs/_quarto/mermaid.lua; the other filters there take page titles from the leading # Heading and point links to non-page files, like main.tf, at GitHub).
Build: .github/workflows/docs-site.yml renders on every push to main that touches Markdown or the site config, and force-pushes _site/ as a single orphan commit to docs-html. Pull requests get a render-only check.
Serve: this stack. docs-site-sync shallow-fetches docs-html every DOCS_SYNC_INTERVAL seconds; nginx serves the result behind a userspace Tailscale sidecar.

The repo is public, so docs-html is public too. That’s the same content as the Markdown it’s built from. GitHub Pages stays off: the site is only hosted on the tailnet. docs/private/ is gitignored, so it never reaches GitHub, CI or this box (CI also fails the build if it shows up).
Rendering in CI rather than on TrueNAS keeps this stack to two tiny images (no ~1 GB Quarto/pandoc image or render job on the NAS) and doubles as a check that the docs still build.

Deploy

Tailscale: it’s an admin-only page, so it uses the existing tag:ts-apps (no ACL change). Create a single-use, pre-approved, non-ephemeral auth key tagged tag:ts-apps.
First build: push to main (or run the docs-site workflow by hand from the Actions tab) so the docs-html branch exists. Check the repo’s Settings → Pages is still disabled.
Dockhand: add the stack pointed at this directory, fill .env from .env.example, deploy. docker logs docs-site-sync should print docs-site: now serving <sha> within a few seconds.
Open https://docs.<tailnet>.ts.net.

title: Docs site
text:
Day to day

Adding a page: new docs/*.md files are picked up by the render glob, but add them to a sidebar section in _quarto.yml so they’re easy to find. New stack READMEs must be added to project.render by name: Quarto skips README.md in globs. CI’s render-list check fails until you do.
Preview locally: quarto preview from the repo root.
Force a refresh: docker restart docs-site-sync.
Upgrades: Renovate bumps the image tags in docker-compose.yml and the Quarto version in the workflow.

title: Games
text:
A ROM library you can browse and play in the browser, plus an *arr that fills it. Tailnet-only:
Prowlarr and qBittorrent are not in this stack. ROMarr uses the ones in arr-stack. igir (for auditing the collection you already have) runs as a one-off command, not a service.

title: Games
text:
Storage layout
Everything sits in the arr-stack media dataset (MEDIA_PATH, e.g. /mnt/tank/media), next to qBittorrent’s downloads/:
tank/media                         ← MEDIA_PATH. ROMarr and qBit both see it as /media
├── downloads/
│   └── games/                     qBit category `romarr` save path
└── games/                         ← a DIRECTORY, not a dataset. RomM sees it as /romm
    ├── library/
    │   ├── roms/<platform>/       RomM Structure A. ROMarr files into here
    │   └── bios/<platform>/       firmware (PS1, Saturn, GBA BIOS, …)
    ├── resources/                 RomM covers/screenshots (rebuildable)
    ├── assets/                    RomM saves, states, screenshots (NOT rebuildable)
    ├── config/                    RomM config.yml (optional)
    └── dats/                      No-Intro + Redump DATs (ROMarr and igir)
apps/games                         ← CONFIG_PATH (SSD)
├── mariadb/                       RomM database
├── romm/redis-data/               RomM's internal Valkey snapshot
└── romarr/                        romarr.json: settings, API key, history
Why games/ must not be a dataset. The arr-stack README’s hardlink rule applies here too. A hardlink can’t cross datasets, and Docker can’t link across two separate bind mounts even on the same dataset. So ROMarr gets the same single ${MEDIA_PATH}:/media mount as qBittorrent. Downloads and the library are then one filesystem on one mount, and qBit’s reported paths (/media/downloads/games/…) mean the same thing inside ROMarr. No remote path mapping is needed.
Platform folders use RomM’s slugs (gba, snes, psx, genesis, …, see RomM’s Supported Platforms page). ROMarr and igir’s {romm} token both produce these names.

title: Games
text:
Reaching Prowlarr and qBittorrent
Both are in the arr-stack Compose project. romarr-ts joins that project’s network (arr-stack_default, declared external), so ROMarr reaches them by service name, http://prowlarr:9696 and http://qbittorrent:8080, the same way Sonarr does. Those URLs are fixed in docker-compose.yml.
Why not the host’s LAN ports: qBittorrent’s killswitch (VPN_LAN_LEAK_ENABLED=false) answers only VPN_LAN_NETWORK and its own Compose network. A request from another Docker bridge to the host’s published :8080 arrives with a bridge source address and gets dropped. Prowlarr’s tailnet name isn’t usable either: the sidecars run in userspace mode, so the app can’t route to other tailnet devices.
Trade-off: deploy arr-stack first; this stack won’t start without its network.

title: Games
text:
Deploy

Tailscale: both are admin-only UIs, so they use the existing tag:ts-apps (no ACL change; group:admin already reaches everything). Create one single-use, pre-approved, non-ephemeral auth key per sidecar, tagged tag:ts-apps.
Directories (TrueNAS shell). Create apps/games with the Apps preset, then:
M=/mnt/tank/media
mkdir -p $M/downloads/games \
         $M/games/library/roms $M/games/library/bios \
         $M/games/resources $M/games/assets $M/games/config $M/games/dats \
         /mnt/apps/games/romm/redis-data /mnt/apps/games/romarr /mnt/apps/games/mariadb
chown -R 568:568 $M/downloads/games $M/games /mnt/apps/games/romm /mnt/apps/games/romarr
zfs list -o name,mountpoint | grep games   # must show apps/games only, NOT tank/media/games
Leave mariadb/ alone. The MariaDB image chowns it on first start.
qBittorrent (arr-stack WebUI): Options → Downloads → enable Automatic Torrent Management as the default. Then right-click Categories → Add category: name romarr, save path /media/downloads/games. ROMarr tags every torrent it adds with this category.
Dockhand: add the stack pointed at this directory and fill the variables from .env.example. Generate ROMM_AUTH_SECRET_KEY with openssl rand -hex 32 and the DB passwords with openssl rand -hex 24. You can’t create the RomM account for ROMarr yet (step 6). Pick its password now and put it in ROMM_ROMARR_PASSWORD, or leave it empty and enter it in ROMarr’s UI later. ROMarr reads its connection variables once, on first start. After that, its Settings pages are what counts. Deploy.
RomM first: open https://romm.<tailnet>.ts.net. The setup wizard creates your admin account.

Metadata: set at least one provider before the first scan. ScreenScraper (artwork, best for retro) and RetroAchievements (hash matching, achievements) are the most useful. IGDB needs a Twitch developer app (client ID + secret). SteamGridDB is covers only. Keys are Dockhand variables (see .env.example); RomM’s Metadata sources page only shows their status. Hasheous, PlayMatch, LaunchBox and HowLongToBeat need no key and are on. Redeploy after adding keys.
Put any BIOS files in games/library/bios/<platform>/.

A dedicated RomM account for ROMarr. ROMarr only reads the catalogue and starts scans. Starting a scan (POST /api/tasks/scan) needs RomM’s tasks.run scope, and in RomM 5.x only the Admin role has it. So:

Administration → Users → add user romarr, role Admin, a long random password.
Preferred: log in as romarr and create a client API token (its profile → API tokens) with only the read scopes plus tasks.run. That token (rmm_…) is all ROMarr gets, so a leak can’t edit or delete your library. Give it to ROMarr as the library API Token (ROMM_API_TOKEN on a first start, or ROMarr’s Libraries page).
Or: give ROMarr the romarr username and password.

Without tasks.run, imports still work, but RomM only notices them at its nightly scan (04:00). ROMarr’s docs call this “The rescan was refused”.
ROMarr: open https://romarr.<tailnet>.ts.net and set a password (unless ROMARR_PASSWORD claimed it already). Then check each Settings page, because first-start seeding only fills in what .env had:

Indexers: Prowlarr, http://prowlarr:9696 + Prowlarr’s API key (Prowlarr → Settings → General). Test.
Download Clients: qBittorrent, http://qbittorrent:8080, your WebUI login, category romarr. Test.
Libraries: RomM, URL http://romm-ts:8080, the token or the romarr login, path /media/games/library/roms, layout Structure A. Run the library test.
Media Management: these settings protect your ratio:

Prefer hardlinks → ON (it is off by default).
Keep completed downloads for seeding after import → ON (default; confirm it).
Use DAT names for verified single-file imports → on.
Overwrite an existing file → off.

Profiles: set preferred regions to Europe, World, USA, Japan (the default is USA first). Leave betas and ROM hacks off.

First game: add a small cartridge game to Wanted, let it grab and import, then check that it’s a hardlink:
ls -li /mnt/tank/media/downloads/games/<release>/<file> \
       /mnt/tank/media/games/library/roms/<platform>/<file>
# Same inode number in column 1 = hardlink, no extra space used.
The torrent should still be Seeding in qBittorrent, and the game should appear in RomM within a minute.

title: Games
text:
Indexers: TorrentLeech and others
ROMarr doesn’t keep its own indexer list. It searches through Prowlarr’s API, across every indexer Prowlarr has, using the Newznab categories 1000 (Console) and 4050 (PC/Games). So you add indexers in Prowlarr, not in ROMarr. Unlike Sonarr, there’s no Prowlarr App to sync.

TorrentLeech is already in Prowlarr with the vpn proxy tag. Check that its category mappings include Console and PC/Games (Prowlarr → Indexers → TorrentLeech → Categories). Grabs go through Prowlarr on the server, so the passkeyed .torrent URL never reaches ROMarr’s UI or logs, and it still goes out through Privoxy.
Others: add any tracker with game categories to Prowlarr the usual way (tag vpn if it needs it). ROMarr picks it up on the next search. The Interactive search page in ROMarr shows which indexer each result came from, which helps check that a new one works.
ROMarr’s Settings → Indexers can also take a Torznab/Newznab feed or a torrent RSS feed directly. Prowlarr is the better place for private trackers, because it handles their auth and the VPN proxy.

ROMarr spaces out its requests (missing-search every 12 h, RSS hourly, and it backs off when an indexer returns HTTP 429), which is what private trackers expect.

title: Games
text:
How quality works
For ROMs, “quality” means “is this a known-good dump?”, not bitrate. The reference for that is a DAT: a checksum list kept by a preservation group.

No-Intro: cartridge and handheld systems (NES … GBA, DS, 3DS decrypted, etc.). Download the daily pack from Dat-o-Matic (datomatic.no-intro.org, free account) → Daily → P/C XML.
Redump: disc systems (PS1, PS2, Saturn, Dreamcast, GameCube, …). Download per system from redump.org/downloads.

Unzip or drop the zips into /mnt/tank/media/games/dats/ (ROMarr reads loose .dat/.xml files and No-Intro’s zips). Keep only DATs in there. ROMarr’s status page warns if it finds anything else. ROMarr rereads the directory on restart.
Each import gets one verdict:








Verdict
Meaning
What ROMarr does




Verified
Every file’s checksum matches a DAT entry.
Files it and, with “Use DAT names”, renames it to the DAT’s canonical name. Search ranks [!] / verified releases higher (+50).


Bad dump
Matches an entry the DAT marks as bad ([b]).
Flags it. Search ranks these down, so a good dump is preferred.


Unknown
No DAT entry matches: missing DAT for the platform, a hack, a translation, a homebrew, a different revision, or a repack.
Files it under its original name. Unknown is not the same as broken. It means nothing here vouches for it.



Collections (in ROMarr) compares a platform folder against its DAT and shows what’s missing. That’s a 1G1R wishlist for one system. Region preference (Profiles) decides which of several releases of the same game counts.

title: Games
text:
Keeping torrents seeding (ratio)
TorrentLeech is private, so a torrent that stops seeding hurts your ratio. How this setup protects it:

Never moved. ROMarr hardlinks (with Prefer hardlinks on) or copies. The setting that matters is Keep completed downloads for seeding after import. In ROMarr 1.10’s code, turning it off makes ROMarr remove the torrent and its files from qBit after a successful import. Keep it on. With it on, ROMarr removes only torrents that never finished (stalled past stalled_timeout_minutes, 180 by default, without deleting files) and paused partial grabs it decided not to use.
Copies instead of links in some cases: archive releases (.zip/.7z ROMs that ROMarr extracts), and ROMs grabbed for a pending request. The copy uses extra space, and the torrent still seeds from the original.
Don’t edit library files in place. A hardlink is one file with two names, so patching or re-zipping the library copy also changes the seeding copy, and the torrent fails its recheck. Renames and deletes are safe (RomM’s renames link + unlink, and deleting in RomM removes only the library name).
Seeding time and ratio are set in qBittorrent (global or the romarr category’s share limits). Set them to at least TorrentLeech’s minimum. Don’t use Remove torrent and its files as the limit action.

title: Games
text:
Importing a set torrent
A set torrent (e.g. a No-Intro pack) holds a whole system’s catalogue. import-romset.sh (next to this README) verifies it against games/dats with igir and files one release per game into library/roms/<platform>/. Copy it to the NAS once, somewhere only root can write (it runs as root):
mkdir -p /root/bin && curl -fsSL -o /root/bin/import-romset.sh \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/H-Mateus/homelab/main/truenas/docker-compose/games/import-romset.sh
chmod 700 /root/bin/import-romset.sh
Then, as root (in tmux: big systems take a while):
/root/bin/import-romset.sh --help
/root/bin/import-romset.sh '/mnt/tank/media/downloads/games/No-Intro 20190501' \
  'Nintendo - Game Boy' 'Sega - Mega Drive - Genesis'

Name the systems as they appear in the download folder, without extension. A folder of per-game zips is hardlinked (no extra space, keeps seeding). A whole-system .rar/.7z of per-game zips is unpacked to games/staging first, because igir can’t read archives inside archives; staging is removed afterwards. The download is mounted read-only.
Curate with --list FILE: one regex per line, matched against the DAT name (^Golden Sun, /mother 3/i). Keep lists in games/lists/.
--dats REGEX limits igir to the DATs whose name matches ("Nintendo DS", "PlayStation 2"). Without it every DAT in games/dats is checked in turn, which is slow with the full No-Intro pack.
--dry-run writes only a report to games/igir-reports/; --all keeps every region, revision, beta and demo.
Needs a DAT for each system: the No-Intro Daily pack (P/C XML) unzipped flat into games/dats, plus Redump DATs for disc systems.
No DAT matches? If the report lists the set’s files as UNUSED (a different dump format from your DAT, e.g. the 2019 DS set, or PS3/Wii U game folders), --no-dat PLATFORM skips igir and hardlinks the files into roms/PLATFORM as they are named: --no-dat nds, ps3, wiiu. RomM still matches them by name and hash.
Then RomM → Scan → Quick scan, or wait for the 04:00 rescan.


Only some games from a huge set (PS1, PS2, …)
A Redump PS2 set is well over 400 GB. Download just a list of games from it with qbit-select.py, which sets the torrent’s file priorities through qBittorrent’s Web API. It needs only Python 3, so run it from this repo on your Mac:

In qBittorrent, add the set’s .torrent file (not a magnet: the file list must be known) with category romarr, unticking “Start torrent”.
Preview, then apply. ps2 is any part of the torrent’s name:
export QBIT_URL=http://truenas-local.<tailnet>.ts.net:8080 QBIT_USER=admin
./qbit-select.py ps2 lists/ps2.txt --dry-run
./qbit-select.py ps2 lists/ps2.txt
For each title it picks one release (all discs, newest revision, no demos or betas) in the --prefer region order, which defaults to USA,World,Europe,UK,Japan: many PAL PS1/PS2 releases run at 50 Hz. Everything else is set to “do not download” and the torrent starts. The dry run lists any line that matched nothing; fix its spelling to the set’s naming.
Lists are cumulative: add a line and re-run to fetch more.
When it finishes, import the folder: import-romset.sh --dats "PlayStation 2" /mnt/tank/media/downloads/games/<set folder>. A set split across torrents (PS2 “A-L” and “M-Z”) is just two torrents: run steps 1-4 on each with the same list. Each dry run reports the other half’s titles as unmatched, which is expected.

lists/ has a starting list per platform (acclaimed games, US titles). Edit them freely. Ratio: TorrentLeech counts only what you download, so unticked files cost nothing; seed what you took for the tracker’s minimum.

title: Games
text:
Converting disc games to CHD
CHD is a lossless disc image format. DuckStation (PS1), PCSX2 (PS2) and PPSSPP (PSP) read it directly, but not the .7z/.zip the sets come in, and it is usually smaller than the raw image. make-chd.sh converts games into library/roms/<platform>/. Install it like import-romset.sh:
curl -fsSL -o /root/bin/make-chd.sh \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/H-Mateus/homelab/main/truenas/docker-compose/games/make-chd.sh
chmod 700 /root/bin/make-chd.sh
/root/bin/make-chd.sh ps2 '/mnt/tank/media/downloads/games/<folder>/<game>.7z'
/root/bin/make-chd.sh ps2 /mnt/tank/media/games/library/roms/ps2/*.7z

No need to wait for seeding. The source is only read. When the same game is already in the library as a hardlink (what import-romset.sh creates), that link is removed and the CHD takes its place; the download keeps seeding. The cost is disk space: the CHD and the download both exist until you remove the torrent.
A library file with no other link (the only copy) is kept; delete it yourself once the CHD plays.
Each .cue (or .gdi) becomes a CD CHD and each .iso a DVD CHD. A patched game converts the same way; it just won’t match any DAT.
Multi-disc games become one CHD per disc.

title: Games
text:
Playing on a PC
RomM’s browser player (EmulatorJS) covers the older systems up to PS1, N64 and DS. PS2, GameCube, Wii, Wii U, 3DS, Xbox, 360 and PS3 need a native emulator. Play those on a PC with ES-DE as the front end and the library mounted read-only from TrueNAS, so every PC sees the same games and nothing is copied.
1. ES-DE folder names (TrueNAS, as root). ES-DE names a few systems differently from RomM (ngc → gc, 3ds → n3ds, sms → mastersystem). esde-view.sh builds library/esde/, one symlink per platform under ES-DE’s name. Re-run it when a new platform folder appears. RomM only reads library/roms, so it ignores esde/.
curl -fsSL -o /root/bin/esde-view.sh \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/H-Mateus/homelab/main/truenas/docker-compose/games/esde-view.sh
chmod 700 /root/bin/esde-view.sh && /root/bin/esde-view.sh
2. Read-only SMB share (TrueNAS UI).

Credentials → Users → Add: user gamer with a password, SMB Access ticked, primary group apps (the library belongs to uid/gid 568). (games is taken: it is a hidden built-in Debian user.)
Shares → Windows (SMB) → Add: path /mnt/tank/media/games/library, name games. Under Advanced Options tick Export Read Only. Save, decline the offer to edit the ACL (permissions stay as they are), and enable the SMB service when asked.

Read-only means nothing on a PC can damage the library. Emulators keep saves and settings locally. The symlinks in esde/ point inside the share, so Samba follows them.
3. Mount it.

CachyOS: sudo pacman -S cifs-utils, put username=gamer and password=… in /etc/smb-games (chmod 600), then add to /etc/fstab:
//192.168.1.2/games /mnt/games cifs ro,credentials=/etc/smb-games,uid=1000,gid=1000,_netdev,nofail,x-systemd.automount 0 0
sudo mkdir /mnt/games && sudo systemctl daemon-reload.
Windows: File Explorer → This PC → Map network drive: Z:, \\192.168.1.2\games, Connect using different credentials, user gamer.

4. ES-DE. Install ES-DE and set its ROM directory to /mnt/games/esde (Linux) or Z:\esde (Windows). Install the emulators below; ES-DE finds them when installed normally (Linux: pacman, Flatpak, or AppImages in ~/Applications; Windows: portable builds in ES-DE’s Emulators folder).

title: Games
section: Auditing your existing collection with igir
text:
Auditing your existing collection with igir
igir checks ROMs against the same No-Intro/Redump DATs, renames them to canonical names, and can sort them straight into RomM’s roms/<platform>/ layout ({romm} token). RomM’s docs describe the same workflow (“igir” under Ecosystem). Run it as a throwaway container on TrueNAS, which has no Node install. Nothing permanent is added.
Set up a helper in the TrueNAS shell (OLD = wherever the existing collection lives):
OLD=/mnt/tank/old-roms            # existing collection — mounted READ-ONLY below
G=/mnt/tank/media/games
mkdir -p $G/igir-reports $G/staging && chown 568:568 $G/igir-reports $G/staging
igir() {
  docker run --rm -it --user 568:568 -e HOME=/tmp \
    -v "$OLD":/old:ro -v "$G":/games \
    node:24-alpine npx -y igir@latest "$@"
}
Step 0: safety net. If OLD is on a dataset, snapshot it first: zfs snapshot <pool/dataset>@pre-igir. The :ro mount already stops any command from changing it.
Step 1: report only (read-only). With report alone igir writes nothing except the CSV:
igir report --dat '/games/dats/*' --input /old \
  --input-checksum-max SHA1 \
  --report-output '/games/igir-reports/audit-%X.csv'
Open the CSV and filter the Status column: - FOUND: a file matches a DAT entry (verified; [b] names are bad dumps). - UNUSED: matched nothing (unknown: hacks, translations, homebrew, headered or trimmed files, or a platform with no DAT loaded). - DUPLICATE: a second copy of something already found. - MISSING: in the DAT but not in your collection. This is long for full sets and is normal.
Step 2: trial build into staging. This copies from the read-only original, so the original is never touched:
igir copy extract test playlist report \
  --dat '/games/dats/*' --input /old \
  --output '/games/staging/roms/{romm}' \
  --input-checksum-max SHA1 \
  --report-output '/games/igir-reports/staging-%X.csv'
test re-verifies every written file. playlist writes .m3u files for multi-disc games.
Optional 1G1R (one game, one ROM: one release per title, picked by region). Add to step 2:
  --single --prefer-language EN --prefer-region UK,EUR,WORLD,USA,JPN \
  --prefer-verified --prefer-good --prefer-retail --prefer-revision newer
and --only-retail to also drop betas, demos, prototypes and unlicensed titles. Note that EU releases of older consoles (NES, SNES, Mega Drive, PS1) are often 50 Hz PAL and run about 17% slower than US versions. For those, try --prefer-region USA,WORLD,UK,EUR,JPN in a separate run per platform. Change --dat to one system’s DAT to limit a run.
Step 3: review, then promote. Browse staging/roms/. Each disc of a multi-disc Redump game lands in its own folder. Move them into one game folder next to the .m3u so RomM shows one game (see RomM’s igir page). Then move it into the library. A move within the same dataset is instant:
cd /mnt/tank/media/games
for d in staging/roms/*/; do p=$(basename "$d"); mkdir -p library/roms/$p; \
  mv -n "$d"* library/roms/$p/; done      # -n: never overwrite something ROMarr filed
Then RomM → Scan (or wait for 04:00). Files still listed as UNUSED in the report weren’t copied. Keep the ones you want (hacks, translations) by copying them into library/roms/<platform>/ by hand. RomM’s subfolder tags (hack, translation) suit them.
Once the new library looks right in RomM, you can delete or archive OLD. Keep the snapshot until you’re sure.

title: Games
text:
Day to day

Want a game: ROMarr → search → add to Wanted (or grab from interactive search). It shows up in RomM after import.
Backups: apps/games (DB, ROMarr state) is covered by the apps snapshot task. games/assets/ holds saves and states, which can’t be re-downloaded. tank/media snapshots are optional in arr-stack, so either snapshot tank/media or back up games/assets/ separately.
Upgrades: Renovate opens a PR bumping the image tags in docker-compose.yml; read the release notes first (RomM: releases, ROMarr: releases). RomM runs DB migrations on start. Back up /mnt/apps/games/romarr/romarr.json before rolling ROMarr back, because older builds drop unknown keys.
Health: ROMarr’s image has a healthcheck (/api/health). Docker marks it unhealthy but doesn’t restart it.

title: Homepage
text: Start page for the homelab (gethomepage.dev): a tile per app with live widgets. Tailnet-only at https://homepage.<tailnet>.ts.net. Complements Uptime Kuma rather than replacing it: Kuma alerts, Homepage is for getting to things.

title: Homepage
text:
Status (deployed 2026-11-02)

Tailscale policy: tag:homepage in tagOwners, plus a grant to the widget targets only (links are opened by the browser, so they need no grant): {"src":["tag:homepage"],"dst":["tag:ts-apps",     "tag:family-jellyfin","tag:immich","tag:paperless",     "tag:truenas-primary","tag:uptime-kuma","tag:homeassistant",     "tag:k8s"],"ip":["tcp:443"]} (last two for the HA and Grafana status dots).
Single-use, pre-approved auth key tagged tag:homepage.
Add the stack in Dockhand pointed at this directory; fill .env from .env.example. Paste the secret values, not the Bitwarden secret IDs (36-char UUIDs), or every widget fails auth.
Check config/ is writable by uid 568 in Dockhand’s checkout (Homepage writes config/logs/).
Fill out config/services.yaml.
Widget keys: Immich (admin account, server.statistics only), Paperless (dedicated view-only homepage user; it must be active, or the token gets “User inactive or deleted”), read-only TrueNAS key.
Kuma status pages: homelab (primary), offsite-box (off-site).
Optional widgets left as links: Navidrome, Frigate, Proxmox, pfSense, Home Assistant (each needs extra creds or TLS handling).
Pin the image to a release (now in docker-compose.yml, bumped by Renovate).

title: Paperless-ngx
text: Document archive for scanned paper. Phone scans go in, get OCR’d, and become searchable. Tailnet-only, at https://paperless.<tailnet>.ts.net.

title: Paperless-ngx
text:
Datasets
apps/paperless            encryption root (key), lz4, recordsize 128K
├── pgdata                child dataset, recordsize 16K   → postgres
├── data/                 dir, 568:568   → search index, classifier, logs
├── media/                dir, 568:568   → originals + archived PDF/A
├── consume/              dir, 568:568   → drop folder (auto-ingested)
└── export/               dir, 568:568   → document_exporter output
Why it’s all on apps (NVMe) and none of it on tank:

Size. Scanned documents are small. Even 10k documents with their archive copies come to tens of GB, and apps has hundreds of GiB free.
Consistency. DB and media share one dataset tree, so one recursive snapshot captures both at the same instant. The DB never points at files the snapshot doesn’t contain.
Backup coverage. The apps snapshot task is already recursive, so the new datasets are picked up automatically. The tank snapshot task is not recursive and would need the dataset added by hand.

Why it’s encrypted: ZFS encryption can only be set when a dataset is created (see docs/at-rest-encryption.md). This is the most sensitive data on the box and it starts out empty, so encrypting now costs nothing. Doing it later means a migration. It also serves as the pilot for the zero-knowledge off-site plan.

Create them (TrueNAS UI)

Datasets → apps → Add Dataset

Name: paperless, Dataset Preset: Generic
Encryption: untick Inherit, tick Encryption, Type Key, Generate Key, Cipher AES-256-GCM
Advanced: Compression LZ4 (inherit), Record Size 128K (inherit), Atime Off

Export the key immediately: apps/paperless → ZFS Encryption card → Export Key. Store it in the password manager and in the offline envelope. The key auto-unlocks at boot from the TrueNAS config DB, so services start unattended. That also means the config backup needs Export Password Secret Seed ticked.
Datasets → apps/paperless → Add Dataset

Name: pgdata, Preset Generic, encryption inherited
Advanced: Record Size 16K. Postgres writes 8K pages, and 16K cuts read-modify-write overhead while staying compressible.

Create the plain directories (TrueNAS shell):
mkdir -p /mnt/apps/paperless/{data,media,consume,export}
chown -R 568:568 /mnt/apps/paperless/{data,media,consume,export}
Leave pgdata owned by root. The postgres entrypoint chowns it to its own uid on first init.



Off-site replication (raw, zero-knowledge)
OpenZFS refuses to send an encrypted dataset with properties unless the send is raw, and one replication task can’t mix raw and non-raw. So Paperless has its own task:

The main “Regular remote backup” PULL task (on Quack01, non-raw into the key-holding HDDs/backups/local) has apps/paperless in Exclude Child Datasets.
A separate PULL task replicates apps/paperless (recursive, same -daily/-weekly/-mothly naming schemas, Encryption unchecked → raw send) to HDDs/backups/paperless. That dataset must NOT be pre-created: the first raw receive creates it as an encrypted copy. It stays locked on Quack01, which never holds the key.

No dedicated snapshot task: the recursive apps snapshot task covers apps/paperless and pgdata.
Restore = replicate back to the primary (or anywhere with the key) and unlock with the exported key.

title: Paperless-ngx
text:
Deploy (Dockhand)

Tailscale admin: add tag:paperless to the ACL. Grant only your own devices; don’t share it with family the way tag:immich is shared. Create a pre-approved, non-ephemeral auth key with that tag.
Dockhand: create the stack from git path truenas/docker-compose/paperless. Fill in .env from .env.example, including PAPERLESS_URL with your tailnet name.
Deploy, open https://paperless.<tailnet>.ts.net, and log in with the admin user. Then blank PAPERLESS_ADMIN_* in Dockhand.

title: Paperless-ngx
text:
Getting documents in

Phone: scan with a document scanner (Google Drive scan, Microsoft Lens) rather than the camera, so you get de-skew and contrast. Then share the PDF to a Paperless mobile app, or upload through the web UI over Tailscale.
Drop folder: anything written to consume/ is ingested and then deleted. It can become an SMB share later, but if so, make consume its own child dataset first so the share’s ACLs don’t touch the rest.

title: Paperless-ngx
text:
Logical backup
Snapshots + replication cover the raw files. On top of that, a nightly export gives you a DB-independent copy you can import into a fresh install. Add it in System → Advanced → Cron Jobs (user root):
docker exec paperless document_exporter ../export --delete --no-progress-bar
Schedule it before the daily apps snapshot, so each snapshot contains a fresh export.

title: Paperless-ngx
text:
Tuning
Capped for the shared NAS: 1 task worker × 2 OCR threads, plus a mem_limit on every container (~2.8 GB in total). Tika + Gotenberg are commented out in the compose file. Enable them only if you need Office documents or .eml ingestion.

title: Reading
text:
Books and manga, fetched automatically and read in one place. Tailnet-only; no LAN ports.
Prowlarr and qBittorrent live in the arr-stack project and are reused here.

title: Reading
text:
Storage
Everything goes in the arr-stack’s media dataset (MEDIA_PATH, e.g. /mnt/tank/media):
tank/media                  MEDIA_PATH
├── downloads/books/        qBittorrent category `books` (save path /media/downloads/books)
├── books/                  Bookshelf root folder (/media/books); Kavita /books
├── manga/                  Suwayomi downloads; Kavita /manga
│   └── mangas/<source>/<series>/<chapter>.cbz
└── comics/                 drop comics in by hand; Kavita /comics
books/ must be a plain directory, not a child dataset. Hardlinks can’t cross datasets (see the arr-stack README, “The hardlink rule”). With a child dataset every import becomes a full copy. That still works, but it doubles the disk used. music/ is a child dataset on purpose; don’t copy that here. manga/ and comics/ could be child datasets because nothing hardlinks into them, but there’s no reason to make them one.
Bookshelf mounts the whole of MEDIA_PATH at /media, the same as qBittorrent. So a path qBittorrent reports (/media/downloads/books/...) exists unchanged inside Bookshelf, and no Remote Path Mapping is needed.
App state (Bookshelf DB, Kavita DB and covers, Suwayomi DB and extensions, Tailscale node keys) lives in CONFIG_PATH (apps/reading), covered by the recursive apps snapshot task.

title: Reading
text:
Setup order

Tailscale: Bookshelf and Suwayomi are admin-only, so their keys use the existing tag:ts-apps. Kavita is family-facing and gets its own tag:family-reading (see “Family access” for the ACL lines). Make three single-use, pre-approved, non-ephemeral auth keys accordingly. Deploy arr-stack first: this stack joins its network.
Datasets and directories (TrueNAS shell):
# apps/reading: create in the UI with the Apps preset, then
mkdir -p /mnt/apps/reading/{bookshelf,kavita,suwayomi}
chown -R 568:568 /mnt/apps/reading
# Library directories (plain mkdir: NOT datasets)
mkdir -p /mnt/tank/media/{books,manga,comics,downloads/books}
chown 568:568 /mnt/tank/media/{books,manga,comics,downloads/books}
Create the directories before the first deploy. Otherwise Docker creates missing bind-mount sources owned by root, and Suwayomi (uid 568) can’t write to manga/.
Dockhand: add the stack pointed at this directory, fill .env from .env.example, deploy.
Bookshelf: follow “Wiring Bookshelf” below.
Suwayomi: add an extension repo, then manga (below).
Kavita: create the admin account and libraries (below), then invite family.

title: Reading
section: Wiring Bookshelf to Prowlarr and qBittorrent
text:
Wiring Bookshelf to Prowlarr and qBittorrent
bookshelf-ts joins arr-stack’s network (arr-stack_default), so the three apps reach each other by name: Bookshelf → prowlarr:9696 and qbittorrent:8080, Prowlarr → bookshelf-ts:8787 (Bookshelf listens inside its sidecar’s namespace, so the sidecar’s name is its address). That’s also how qBittorrent’s VPN killswitch lets it through: it answers its own Compose network, which a request to the host’s published port wouldn’t come from.

Bookshelf (first login at https://bookshelf.<tailnet>.ts.net)

Create the login when prompted (Forms auth).
Settings → Media Management (Show Advanced):

Root folder: /media/books.
Use Hardlinks instead of Copy: on. Completed torrents are then hardlinked into books/ and keep seeding from downloads/books/. Bookshelf never moves a torrent that is still seeding, but this keeps the “copy” from costing disk.

Settings → Download Clients → + → qBittorrent:

Host qbittorrent, port 8080, plus the qBittorrent WebUI login (or API key on qBittorrent 5.2+).
Category books. In qBittorrent, set the books category’s save path to /media/downloads/books, next to the other categories.
Remove Completed: off. TorrentLeech is a ratio tracker. Let qBittorrent’s own share limits decide when a torrent stops, not Bookshelf.

title: Uptime Kuma
text:
Uptime checks, alerts and a status page for the homelab. Two copies that watch each other:
Both run this directory’s docker-compose.yml; only .env differs (see .env.example). Quack01’s Dockhand is a separate instance, not an agent of the primary’s: the off-site box must not be controllable from the primary (backups are pulled by Quack01 for the same reason).
Why two: the primary copy can’t tell you the house is offline, because its alerts have to leave via the house’s internet connection. The off-site copy sees that from outside. Each one monitors the other, so either dying alerts from the survivor.
Kuma deliberately runs outside the Talos cluster: the cluster (and Grafana) are among the things it watches.

title: Uptime Kuma
text:
Deploy

Tailscale ACL (admin console): add the tag and let it reach what it monitors.
"tagOwners": { "tag:uptime-kuma": ["autogroup:admin"] },
"grants": [
  { "src": ["tag:uptime-kuma"], "dst": ["*"], "ip": ["tcp:443", "tcp:80", "tcp:8006", "icmp:*"] }
]
Narrow dst to specific tags later if you prefer.
Auth keys: two single-use, pre-approved, non-ephemeral keys tagged tag:uptime-kuma.
Primary: create dataset apps/uptime-kuma, add the stack in Dockhand pointed at this directory, fill .env from .env.example, deploy.
Off-site: create dataset HDDs/uptime-kuma with data/ and ts-state/ inside, add the stack in Quack01’s Dockhand pointed at this directory, and fill .env with KUMA_ROOT=/mnt/HDDs/uptime-kuma/data, TS_HOSTNAME=uptime-offsite, TS_STATE_PATH=/mnt/HDDs/uptime-kuma/ts-state and the auth key. (It was a TrueNAS “Install via YAML” app until 2026-10-31; the data and Tailscale state carried over in place.)
Open https://uptime.<tailnet>.ts.net and https://uptime-offsite.<tailnet>.ts.net and create the admin user on each straight away.
Check MagicDNS works from inside Kuma: add an HTTP monitor for another *.ts.net service. If it can’t resolve, use the device’s 100.x address.

Primary (uptime)

https://uptime-offsite.<tailnet>.ts.net — the other watcher.

Off-site (uptime-offsite)

https://uptime.<tailnet>.ts.net — the primary watcher.
A few signals that mean “the house is up”: Home Assistant, Immich, the primary TrueNAS.
Ping pfsense.<tailnet>.ts.net (pfSense’s Tailscale package, tag:pfsense; 60 s, 3 retries): fails if the house’s internet, the router or the power is down.

Both: a dead man’s switch on healthchecks.io (free). Make one check per Kuma (period 1 min, grace 5 min) with its own alert channel, then add a plain HTTP monitor in each Kuma pointed at that check’s ping URL — every run doubles as a heartbeat. (Not a Kuma Push monitor: that waits to be pinged, the wrong direction.) If both copies are down at once (e.g. a power cut), healthchecks.io notices the missing heartbeats.
